tropes.name: Wicked Pretentious
tropes.html: It's noted that the oldest and most experienced wiseguys try to seem the most respectable but also wear the cheapest suits. This is deliberate on their part; they want you to know they are accustomed to getting their hands dirty and respectability hasn't changed that.

tropes.name: Wife-Basher Basher
tropes.html: Sonny Corleone, in spite of being an unfaithful husband, does not tolerate men hitting women. ESPECIALLY when it comes to his sister: "If you touch my sister again I'll kill you!". Unfortunately this is used to lure him to his death.

tropes.name: Wounded Gazelle Gambit
tropes.html: How the Corleones ultimately prevail over the other families. Following the death of Sonny, Vito holds a peace treaty where he concedes to all of the other dons' demands, making it appear as though his family is no longer in any shape to fight. In the years that follow, he and Michael instruct their men to not fight back as the other families encroach on their territory (further giving off the illusion of weakness). This causes the other dons to abandon all caution and loosen their security, allowing Michael's assassins to kill all of them in one fell swoop.

tropes.name: Xanatos Gambit
tropes.html: Barzini's plot has Tattaglia send Sollozzo to the Corleones to see about increasing the drug traffic. If Vito says yes then the drug trade can begin immediately (with the backing of the Corleones' extensive political contacts), but if he says no, Sollozzo will sow discord within the Corleone ranks. If Sollozzo fails to sway the Corleone family and all out war breaks out (which it does), the Corleones will spend their time gunning for Sollozzo and Tattaglia. Any way it plays out, Barzini wins. It almost works except that Vito figures out "It was Barzini all along."

tropes.name: You Owe Me
tropes.html:
Vito's standard approach to business binding.
Vito: Some day, and that day may never come, I will call upon you to do a service for me. But until that day, consider this justice a gift on my daughter's wedding day.

title: The Godfather Part III

accept.reason: "The Godfather Part III is the final film of The Godfather gangster film trilogy ... Released in 1990": one film; the word trilogy trips the shared-page rule

intro: The Godfather Part III is the final film of The Godfather gangster film trilogy, directed by Francis Ford Coppola and co-written by Coppola and Mario Puzo like the previous films. Released in 1990, the film was intended to serve more as a coda rather than a true sequel to the first two films from the 70s, but Coppola and Puzo's preferred title The Death of Michael Corleone was rejected by Paramoun

tropes.name: Artistic License – History
tropes.html:
• The deaths of Pope Paul VI and John Paul I take place in 1979, the year after their real-life deaths. Furthermore, the name of the actual Cardinal who becomes John Paul I appears to have been changed, along with his pre-papal posting in Sicily rather than Venice. This overlaps with Very Loosely Based on a True Story, since the movie is based on several conspiracy theories surrounding the death of the real-life John Paul I and offers an accordingly fictionalized version of events. Also, Pope John Paul I appears to die on the same night as the opera, which was stated to premiere at Easter. Easter takes place in April or late March, depending on the year. John Paul I died in late September.
    • It's implied that the Cardinal Karol Wojtyła (the future John Paul II) was the Cardinal to ask John Paul I if he accepted election and what papal name he would use. In both 1978 conclaves Cardinal Jean-Marie Villot was the one who asked the winners if they accepted election and what name they would use, as he was the most senior cardinal bishop.

tropes.name: Bad Habits
tropes.html: This guise fails as the old mafia boss recognises the assassin sent to kill his guest Michael Corleone.

tropes.name: Beautiful Singing Voice
tropes.html: Michael's son Anthony drops out of college to become a professional singer, and is good enough to get third billing in an opera within a year.

tropes.name: Board to Death
tropes.html: The board meeting becomes a massacre when a helicopter shows up and shoots at everyone.

tropes.name: Composite Character
tropes.html: Francis Ford Coppola describes Vincent as this, having Vito's cunning, Michael's ruthlessness, Fredo's sensitivity, Sonny's temper, and Tom's loyalty.

tropes.name: Concert Climax
tropes.html: The ending takes place at an opera and involves an assassination attempt. The target is Michael who survives, but his beloved daughter is killed.

tropes.name: Confessional
tropes.html:
Michael gets to confess and receive absolution from the future Pope John Paul I himself.
His Holiness: "Your sins are terrible. And it is just that you suffer. Your life could be redeemed, but I know you do not believe that. You will not change."

tropes.name: Corrupt Church
tropes.html: One of the central stories of the film involves the Vatican City bank getting involved with the Mafia, with The Pope as a reformist.

tropes.name: Death Wail
tropes.html: Michael Corleone's full scream when Mary dies was supposedly so primal and intense that a good chunk of the full audio had to be cut from the movie.

tropes.name: Distant Finale
tropes.html: The final scene takes place in 1997, showing a lone Michael long after the plot of the movie.

tropes.name: Dull Surprise
tropes.html: Mary gets shot outside of a theater, and all she pulls off is a rather flat and expressionless "Dad?"

tropes.name: Dying Alone
tropes.html: In stark contrast to Vito, Michael dies alone surrounded by idle dogs, which serves to underscore his tragic failure.

tropes.name: Eternal Grief at the End
tropes.html: At the opera, Michael witnesses Mary gunned down by an assassin that was meant for him. As he cradles her lifeless body in his arms, he relives his life with her by his side through flashback, and realizing that he led her to her death, lets loose a silent, but greatly anguished scream of pure pain. This moment haunts Michael for the rest of his life as he withdraws from the public eye and dies alone in Sicily, slumped over in his chair, a hollow shell of the man he was.

tropes.name: Exact Words
tropes.html: At the end, Michael makes a solemn vow on the souls of his children that he will never sin again and retires as Godfather. He then names as his successor someone who he knows will start off his reign with a bloody purge of his enemies the same way that Michael once did. God apparently doesn't approve of the Loophole Abuse, as on the same night as the purge, Michael's daughter is killed while her brother helplessly watches.

tropes.name: Facepalm
tropes.html: Michael does one, muttering "Oh, Jesus..." after Vincent bites off Joey Zasa's ear.

tropes.name: Fake Defector
tropes.html: After identifying Don Altobello as the traitor, Michael puts Vincent under Altobelo's tutelage. Michael takes some precautions to avoid an obvious identification of the trope.

tropes.name: Fate Worse than Death
tropes.html: The Godfather, Coda: The Death of Michael Corleone has the titular demise be symbolic rather than literal as in Part III. Instead of dying, the ending has him live a long life alone, and haunted by his failures.

tropes.name: Fictionalized Death Account
tropes.html: Part III RetCons the death of Pope John Paul I and the murder of the Vatican's chief banker into parts of a Mafia vs. Vatican conspiracy. Assuming they weren't in the first place.

tropes.name: Following in Relative's Footsteps
tropes.html:
Defied in Part III, Anthony explicitly tells Michael he has no wish to be like him:
I will always be your son, but I will never have anything to do with your business.

tropes.name: Happy Flashback
tropes.html: The final scene of the saga is preceded by a montage reprising Michael's happy moments with the women of his life, including dancing with his daughter Mary.

tropes.name: Historical Domain Character
tropes.html: The film features Pope John Paul I as a major character and climaxes near his election to the papacy in the Sistine Chapel. Downplayed in that he's fictionalized to the point where his pre-papal name is different (Lamberto in the film, Albino Luciani in real life).

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html: The film follows Michael, being at the cusp of genuinely going legitimate, trying his best to seal the deal, only for enemies and circumstances to render said efforts all for nought.

tropes.name: Impersonating an Officer
tropes.html: Vincent pretends to be a cop to get close enough to an unsuspecting Joey Zasa to assassinate him.

tropes.name: Improvised Weapon
tropes.html: In Part III, Don Lucchesi is assassinated in a truly spectacular fashion when he is stabbed in the throat with his own glasses.

tropes.name: It's Not You, It's My Enemies
tropes.html:
The main reason why Michael dislikes Vincent and Mary dating, and convinces Vincent to break off the romance. It leads to break her heart to save her. It does not work out in the end.
Mary: I'll always love you.
Vincent: Love somebody else.

tropes.name: Just a Gangster
tropes.html: The film shows that not everyone within the Corleone Family is pleased with Michael's efforts to turn the Family legit, and Joey Zasa in particular is recruited by enemies from outside the Family to undermine it from within.

tropes.name: Kissing Cousins
tropes.html: Michael's daughter, Mary, and nephew, Vincent, are in love. Michael is against their relationship, but Mary's mother, Kay, is not. However, Michael's objections are apparently not based on consanguinity, but the danger of Vincent's lifestyle.

tropes.name: Man Bites Man
tropes.html: Vincent (Sonny's bastard son) bites Joey Zasa's ear in their meeting, more proof of Generation Xerox.

tropes.name: Man of Wealth and Taste
tropes.html: Joey Zasa in Part III likes to be known for his well-dressed style (he's even been dubbed "best-dressed gangster" by Esquire magazine) and as a champion of Italian-American heritage. It doesn't exactly endear him to his fellow mafiosi.

tropes.name: Meaningful Echo
tropes.html: During his meeting with Michael at the beginning, Joey Zasa tells Michael that he "has a stone in his shoe", referencing his troubling subordinate Vincent Mancini. Later, Don Altobello uses the exact same phrase while conferring with Mosca de Montelepre, the assassin Altobello hires to kill Michael. This provides subtle (if superfluous, by this point) confirmation that Zasa and Altobello are in league to destroy Don Corleone.

tropes.name: The Mole
tropes.html: The series' recurring plot twist is present with Joey Zasa as a too-obvious opponent that Michael quickly discerns as a front for hidden and more dangerous enemies: it is really Don Altobello working in league with the European banking interests to get Michael's vast wealth put into the Vatican banks.

tropes.name: More Dakka
tropes.html: A meeting between prominent families is interrupted by a helicopter with a machinegun. It is a bloodbath.

tropes.name: Next Sunday A.D.
tropes.html: The final scene is set in 1997, seven years after the film's original release.

tropes.name: No Celebrities Were Harmed
tropes.html:
• Joey Zasa is based on John Gotti, and his demise in his Italian-American pride parade is based on Joe Columbo.
  • Don Lucchesi is based on Italian politician Giulio Andreotti. Archbishop Gilday and Frederick Keinszig are based on other figures in the Vatican Bank scandals, Paul Marcinkus and Roberto Calvi.

tropes.name: Older and Wiser
tropes.html: Connie is practically The Load in her younger years since the business is not female-friendly, but she evolves and by now she is Lady Macbeth.

tropes.name: Pre-Mortem One-Liner
tropes.html: "Power wears out those who don't have it." This doubles as an ironic Historical In-Joke, since the original phrase was coined by Giulio Andreotti, the inspiration for Don Lucchesi.

tropes.name: Re-Cut
tropes.html: For the film's 30th Anniversary in 2020, a new cut of the film called Mario Puzo's The Godfather, Coda: The Death of Michael Corleone was created by Francis Ford Coppola for a limited theatrical release before hitting home media. This version contains a new beginning and ending alongside other changes to better align with Coppola and Puzo's original intentions.

tropes.name: Redemption Rejection
tropes.html: As his priest puts it, while Michael can be forgiven for his sins, as long as Michael himself does not believe he can earn forgiveness, he will never truly change his ways.

tropes.name: Ripped from the Headlines
tropes.html: The "Mafia money laundering at the Vatican" plot in based on the Vatican Bank scandal of 1981—82.

tropes.name: Save You From Becoming Your Parent
tropes.html:
• Kay confronts Michael to allow their son Anthony to abandon his law studies and pursue a musical career. Michael is legit by then and needs lawyers, but he graciously concedes.
  • Michael explicitly mentors Vincent to avoid the mistakes of Santino, his father.
    "But his temper. Clouded his judgment. I don't want to see the same thing happen to you."
    "Never hate your enemies. It affects your judgment."

tropes.name: Say My Name
tropes.html:
When Vincent assassinates Joey Zasa, he makes sure to call out his victim's name as he does the deed.
Vincent: "How are you, Joe... [he shoots Zasa thrice] ZASA!"

tropes.name: The Scream
tropes.html: When his daughter Mary is fatally shot during a hit meant for him, Michael delivers a wail that is so heartrending most of it had to be muted in both versions.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: Michael notes that Joey Zasa has been named "Best-Dressed Gangster" by Esquire magazine.

tropes.name: Tampering with Food and Drink
tropes.html: The poisoned cannolis that Connie serves to assassinate Don Altobello.

tropes.name: Tempting Fate
tropes.html: Played for Tragedy. Michael really should not "Swear by the lives of my children I will sin no more" and then order a final slew of assassinations.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Badass
tropes.html: After being the least important of the Corleone siblings In-Universe (what with being a woman and all that) and a Domestic Abuse victim in the previous films, Connie temporarily replaces Michael as family boss when he falls ill in the middle of a gang war. She also fatally poisons Don Altobello, the Big Bad of Part III.

tropes.name: Undignified Death
tropes.html: Played for Drama. The 1990 cut ends with Michael, alone (aside from two dogs), shattered and having alienated everybody who ever cared about him, slowly falling off his chair, with the dogs running near him, in contrast with his father Vito, who died at a family gathering in his garden, playing with his grandson in his final moments.

tropes.name: Villain with Good Publicity
tropes.html: Kay accuses Michael of Hiding Behind Religion when Michael is knighted by the Church.

tropes.name: Villainous Breakdown
tropes.html: When Mary gets shot, Michael screams with such primal fury that he induces a stroke.

tropes.name: Yank the Dog's Chain
tropes.html: In the end, Michael has successfully turned his criminal enterprises over to his nephew and transitioned himself to working in completely legal business. His children are totally clean, with his daughter the head of a charity foundation and his son an opera singer. As young Tony makes his triumphant debut performance, Michael notes to himself that the Corleone name has escaped its past, and now will be remembered for a voice. Then a hitman that Vincent's people failed to catch during the opera opens fire, wounding Michael and accidentally killing Mary.

title: The Hangover

intro: The Hangover is an American comedy film released in 2009 directed by Todd Phillips and is the first installment in The Hangover (Film Series). The plot follows these four guys drive to Las Vegas for a bachelor party, and the bulk of the film deals with three of the friends (Ed Helms, Bradley Cooper, and Zach Galifianakis) trying to remember the events of the previous night while trying to track do

tropes.name: Accidental Marriage
tropes.html: Because you can't have a party in Las Vegas without somebody taking a spontaneous trip down the aisle.

tropes.name: Air Drums
tropes.html:
Mike Tyson, when the guys are in his hotel room.
Mike: Shh, shh... This is my favorite part coming up right now.

tropes.name: Alcohol-Induced Idiocy
tropes.html: Obviously. Except it's not from alcohol, it's from being unknowingly drugged.

tropes.name: Animeland
tropes.html:
When a naked, angry Asian man jumps out of the trunk of the car, Alan instantly tries to calm him down by saying that he hates Godzilla too.
  • If you pay attention to Chow's face, it can become a funny moment: he leaves because he's just so confused by the Godzilla line.

tropes.name: Anywhere but Their Lips
tropes.html: Among the first clues that Stu's girl really isn't right for him is that she won't let him kiss her on the lips.

tropes.name: Apathetic Teacher
tropes.html: Phil pretty much doesn't give a rat's ass about the kids in his class.

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Question
tropes.html: When Stu is confronted by Melissa, she angrily asks him why he went to Las Vegas. This causes Melissa to breakdown and shout at him, causing them to break up.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Law
tropes.html: Needing a large amount of money to get Doug back, the trio go to a blackjack table where Alan wins over $80,000 by counting cards, despite the other guys telling him earlier it's illegal. The thing is, Alan's method of counting cards was not illegal. He didn't use any outside devices or receive instructions from a partner, so he didn't break any laws.

tropes.name: Asian Rudeness
tropes.html: Leslie Chow qualifies, with his aggressiveness and insults.

tropes.name: Beast in the Building
tropes.html: The main characters wake up after a blackout drunk bachelor party to a trashed hotel suite full of unexplained items, including a live chicken. When Alan goes to the bathroom, it takes him a moment to realize there's a tiger with him. They stole it from Mike Tyson.

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html: Mike Tyson as himself. Also Carrot Top and Wayne Newton during the end credits photo montage.

tropes.name: Catchphrase
tropes.html:
Phil says "No shit it's X" often enough during the course of the movie for it to count as one.
  • Phil also says "No, this is good!" every time they remember something terrible from the night before. Stu eventually calls him on it.
  • Alan: "That's classic!"
  • Stu: "WHAT THE FUCK IS GOING ON?!"

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• Or his ring, in this case. As soon as the Holocaust ring is introduced, you know something is going to happen to it. Stu uses it when he gets married to a hooker.
  • Also, the "This Door Locks Behind You" sign on the door to the roof was a pretty obvious sign that somebody was getting locked up there at some point — though by the time they found Doug, it had long been forgotten.. Possibly a Brick Joke.
  • The tiger. Mike Tyson's tiger.
  • Alan's card counting book, which leads to the Chekhov's Skill.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html: As the guys are waking up, a woman is leaving the room. It turns that she actually married Stu the night before.<!--* ChekhovsSkill: Card-counting.-->

tropes.name: Comically Missing the Point
tropes.html: Stu is more concerned that his friends get it right who his girlfriend cheated on him with (a bartender, not a bellhop) than with the fact that she cheated on him in the first place.

tropes.name: Cool Car
tropes.html: You'll never see a finer example of a 1969 Mercedes-Benz convertible on film. Too bad they gradually smash the shit out of it as the movie goes on.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
tropes.html: Director Todd Phillips is the man they walk in on going down on his girlfriend in the elevator.

tropes.name: Danger Takes a Backseat
tropes.html: In the form of a tiger, although they put it in there.

tropes.name: Delayed "Oh, Crap!"
tropes.html: Happens to Alan near the start. He goes into the suite's bathroom and doesn't notice the tiger in the room with him at first. When he does, he merely turns away and mutters, "Stupid tiger." Seconds later, cue the Oh, Crap! when he realizes that yes, there is definitely a tiger in the bathroom with him. Cue a hasty exit and frantically warning the others not to go in there.

tropes.name: Destroy the Evidence
tropes.html: The film ends with Alan discovering his digital camera in the car and finding it contains pictures of all the bachelor party shenanigans the group couldn't remember. They agree to view the pictures together one time and then delete them so there's no evidence.

tropes.name: The Ditz
tropes.html: Jade plays this during Alan's second blackjack haul.

tropes.name: DIY Dentistry
tropes.html: Stu is missing a tooth when they wake up from the night they can't remember. At the end, it's revealed that he pulled it out himself because the others said he couldn't do it. For extra irony points, Stu himself is a dentist, for all the difference it makes when yanking out a tooth with pliers at a strip club while black-out drunk.

tropes.name: The Dog Bites Back
tropes.html: After being cheated on, humiliated, and beaten by Melissa throughout the film, Stu finally decides to stand up for himself and subsequently breaks up with her.

tropes.name: Double Standard: Abuse, Female on Male
tropes.html: Subverted with Stu's shrill, unfaithful and physically abusive fiancé Melissa. On the one hand, it's played as Black Comedy, but pretty much everyone but him in the story agrees that she's rotten. Even when Stu stands up to her at the end, she seems rather flippant about it. Seeing him finally break up with her in a rather magnificent (albeit awkward) manner is one of the most satisfying moments in the film.

tropes.name: Dude, Not Funny!
tropes.html: Invoked with Mike Tyson's reaction to Phil dry humping his tiger.

tropes.name: Early-Installment Weirdness
tropes.html: In the first film, Chow is treated as more of a mafia boss or the head of a crime syndicate, complete with henchmen and very hands off way of doing things. All other appearances have him working alone and make it pretty clear that he's way too kooky to be in charge of anyone.

tropes.name: "Eureka!" Moment
tropes.html: How Stu figures out where Doug is.

tropes.name: Fan Disservice
tropes.html:
• Alan's naked ass. Even worse, his dick gets sucked by an elderly woman in the credits.
  • And when we thought it couldn't get any worse than that, a wrinkled, overweight old man gets a physical exam in front of the heroes, and we're subjected to a shot of his backside as well.
  • Mr. Chow popping out of the trunk, totally naked, his already small penis obscured by a lion's-mane of pubic hair.

tropes.name: Fanservice
tropes.html:
• Phil waking up without a shirt on. Also, when he wears that black suit.
  • Heather Graham whipping her tit out. Also, all the naked women in the photos that play over the credits.
  • The numerous shots of women in their bikinis at the pool.

tropes.name: Fiery Cover-Up
tropes.html: After visiting the chapel, Stu suggests taking all the merchandise from his Shotgun Wedding to Jade, putting it in the cop car, and torching the cop car. Phil has to talk him down from that.

tropes.name: Finish Him!
tropes.html: The male cop screams this while goading a kid to taser Phil.

tropes.name: Forgotten First Meeting
tropes.html: Played for Laughs. Phil doesn't recognize Alan when he meets him and Doug for the bachelor party. Alan reminds him he's met Phil four times.

tropes.name: Groin Attack
tropes.html:
• Phil gets zapped in the crotch during the tasering class.
  • Mr Chow hits Stu in the crotch with a crowbar.

tropes.name: HA HA HA—No
tropes.html: Chow: "HA-HA-HA-HA- ahhh, fuck you."

tropes.name: Hero Antagonist
tropes.html: The cops.

tropes.name: Homage
tropes.html:
To Rain Man, when Alan gets their money back.
Phil: Don't you have to be really smart to count cards?
Alan: Oh yeah? Someone should tell that to Rain Man. He nearly bankrupt Vegas and he was a "ruh-TARD."

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html: When the three amigos win their $80,000 back and are celebrating that they'll now get Doug back. Then the trade happens.

tropes.name: How We Got Here
tropes.html: Pretty much the whole movie, after Phil calls Doug's fiance.

tropes.name: Hypocritical Humor
tropes.html: Ambiguously Gay Mr. Chow referring to the heroes as "gayboys".

tropes.name: I'm a Doctor, Not a Placeholder
tropes.html: The doctor that treated Phil says "I'm a doctor, not a tour guide" when asked about the directions of the chapel.

tropes.name: Insistent Terminology
tropes.html:
• Alan's bag; Phil call it a man-purse, and Alan insists it's a satchel. He later gets into an argument with Chow on the matter.
    It's not a purse, it's a satchel. Indiana Jones wears one.
  • "It was a bartender!"

tropes.name: Instant-Win Condition
tropes.html: Despite all the terrible, terrible consequences of all their activities in Vegas, when the main characters find Doug and return him (mostly) on time to the wedding, that's it, conflict over. They even ended up winning $80,000 that Doug managed to hold on to. Of course, they did blackmail the cops into letting them go without jail timenote though the third film shows that the arrest was documented, as a police officer explicitly mentions it when reading Stu and Phil's records (but not without hilarious results), Mike Tyson forgives them for the tiger incident, Jade acknowledges the marriage as stupid and allows Stu to leave, and the Triads/Yakuza/whatever the hell a Korean Mafia is called only wanted the money.

tropes.name: Irritation Is the Sincerest Form of Flattery
tropes.html: By the end of the film, Alan's taken to mimicking Phil. When Phil realizes this, as they wait for Stu so they can leave, his expression looks like a non-verbal Flat "What".

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html: Stu's girlfriend Melissa and the two cops who got their cruiser stolen by the Wolfpack.

tropes.name: Just Keep Driving
tropes.html: When they are taking the tiger back to Mike Tyson's house and they hit the bus, then stop the car in the middle of the road. None of the other vehicles bother to stop.

tropes.name: Lyrical Dissonance
tropes.html: Singing a rap song during a wedding? Fine. Maintaining its sexually explicit lyrics, f-word and all? Hilarious.

tropes.name: Megaphone Gag
tropes.html: After the protagonists get stuck in traffic in their stolen police car, the driver activates the lights and siren and demands pedestrians get out of the way so they can drive on the sidewalk. At the end of the scene, he addresses a female pedestrian and says "Ma'am in the leopard dress, you have an amazing rack" over the speaker system.

tropes.name: Never Trust a Trailer
tropes.html: You'd think Mike Tyson punched Alan's lights out right at the peak of the climax to "In the Air Tonight" by watching the trailer. But in the final cut, Mike finishes the song, and Alan is knocked out later in that scene.

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html: Turns out Alan spiked the group's rooftop drinks with what he believed was ecstasy because he wanted to ensure they all had a good time. Unfortunately, the dealer accidentally gave him roofies and the drinks instead caused them all to suffer memory loss.

tropes.name: One-Steve Limit
tropes.html: An important plot point is that there are two characters named Doug — a drug dealer who sold the roofies to Alan, and the lost groom. They wind up inadvertently rescuing the first Doug, who inspires a "Eureka!" Moment, which leads to them finding Doug on the roof.

tropes.name: Ontological Mystery
tropes.html: Three friends wake up in a Vegas hotel room with serious hangovers and no memory of what happened last night. One of their friends is missing and there are signs of them having been involved in some kind of wild party. From there the rest of the film is about the trio investigating to figure out just what the hell happened.

tropes.name: Plot Armor
tropes.html:
• Among other things, how Doug survived spending 36 hours on the roof of a Vegas hotel without water and minimal shade.
  • The gang as a whole takes a huge amount of punishment and keeps on going, despite also being extremely hungover. Special mention goes to Alan, who repeatedly takes blows to the head (including from Mike Tyson himself), and seems none the worse for wear.

tropes.name: Red Herring
tropes.html:
• You'd really think that Alan's comment about not being allowed within 200 feet of schools or Chuck-E-Cheeses was going to come back to haunt them later in the movie.
  • Stu's missing tooth might count. It seemed like it would be just as much of a clue as all the other weird stuff they found, but it turns out it doesn't have any relevance to finding Doug. Stu just pulled it out himself for a dare.
  • Not mention when they hear the banging in the trunk.

tropes.name: "The Reason You Suck" Speech
tropes.html: Stu gives one of these to Melissa at the end of the film, to Phil's delight.

tropes.name: Running Gag
tropes.html:
Two instances of Insistent Terminology.
  • "He was a bartender!" (And he didn't even cum inside of Melissa.)
  • "You're a dentist, not a doctor."

tropes.name: "Shaggy Dog" Story
tropes.html: Downplayed. The trio probably would've found Doug a lot quicker had they not been misinformed about Doug's mattress being thrown out of the window when it was actually thrown off the roof, but there was still the matter of the tiger, baby, etc.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• The wedding singer is the same one from Phillips' Old School and Starsky & Hutch.
  • Also, Gremlins is referenced in the dialogue.
  • The tiger found in the found bathroom is a reference to the leopard in the bathroom in Bringing Up Baby.
  • Alan obliquely refers to Three Men and a Baby when they meet up with Jade.
  • The scene in the desert with the protagonists' car reflected in Mr Chow's sunglasses is a direct reference to Casino (also set in Vegas).
  • Three men sitting in a car, then hearing a thumping sound from a person in the trunk might also invoke memories of GoodFellas, another Scorsese film.
  • Tommy Boy: The tiger waking up and destroying the Cool Car is a direct echo of this, especially the shot of the animal pausing to kick out the window.
  • "What happened to Omar?" "Don't worry about Omar, he's not with us no more."
  • And the Rain Man tribute in the casino complete with the same actress in the casino scene in that movie wearing the same dress.
  • One of the songs used in the soundtrack is Kanye West's "Can't Tell Me Nothing", which Galifinakis created an alternate music video for in 2007.

tropes.name: Spoiler Cover
tropes.html: On the poster, Phil has scratches on the side of his neck, which he gets when he gets attacked by the tiger while driving the car.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Spoil
tropes.html: The DVD commercial points out the One-Steve Limit.

tropes.name: Trespassing to Talk
tropes.html: The trio come back to their hotel room to find Mike Tyson waiting for them and their explanation as to why they have his tiger.

tropes.name: Unwitting Instigator of Doom
tropes.html:
• The events may have been avoided if the drug dealer didn't accidentally give Alan roofies instead of ecstasy.
  • The three may have found Doug earlier had the valet not misinformed them about Doug's mattress being thrown out of the window, when it was actually thrown off the roof.

tropes.name: Visual Calculus
tropes.html: When Alan begins card counting during a game of blackjack, advanced calculus manifests briefly to surround him.

tropes.name: Viva Las Vegas!
tropes.html: Trope Exemplar.

tropes.name: Vomit Indiscretion Shot
tropes.html: Three of them, although one's a still photo during the end credits and another is in black and white so only one is really gross.

tropes.name: Wasn't That Fun?
tropes.html:
After Alan almost navigates them into a semi truck on the freeway while they're driving to Vegas.
Alan: "That was awesome!"
Doug: "That was NOT awesome, what is wrong with you?!"

tropes.name: Watch the Paint Job
tropes.html: Since the Mercedes is The Precious, Precious Car, of course it'll be wrecked beyond recognition.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html:
• Some viewers were preoccupied the entire movie with just the mystery of the chicken (which is never really resolved), a very minor detail. According to Todd Phillips in the DVD commentary, the group stole the chicken so they could feed it to the tiger.
  • We also never truly find out what landed Phil in the hospital.
    • In the credits, he's slapped by the tiger.
  • We never find out where the sword stuck into the couch came from either.
  • Why the chair wound up on fire is never explained either

tropes.name: What Did I Do Last Night?
tropes.html: The main characters spend the whole movie trying to figure out the answer to this question. The answer? Everything you can do in Vegas, and then some.

tropes.name: Where It All Began
tropes.html: The guys finally find Doug on the hotel roof, where the whole night started. In fact, they really had all the clues they needed within a few minutes of figuring out he was gone.

title: Puss in Boots

accept.reason: Main/PussInBoots lists it as "The film about the Shrek character, Puss in Boots (2011)"; its intro has no medium word; Wikidata P6839 WesternAnimation/PussInBoots redirects to that list

intro: Before he was a hired hitman, Puss in Boots (Antonio Banderas) was a swashbuckling outlaw who was forced to leave his hometown of San Ricardo. Several years after he left, Puss reunites with Humpty Alexander Dumpty (Zach Galifianakis), a fellow orphan turned thief whose betrayal turned Puss from hero to villain in the eyes of San Ricardo's citizens. Puss is still resentful of his former friend and

tropes.name: Abandonment-Induced Animosity
tropes.html:
• Kitty Softpaws' owners declawed and abandoned her. This is the reason she has trust issues (and a nasty habit of backstabbing people), though it turns out that once you gain her trust, she's quite loyal.
  • Humpty Dumpty, it turns out, is pretty sore at his titular childhood blood brother and old friend for abandoning him during a botched robbery years ago; albeit one which Humpty outright deceived Puss into accidentally committing, which ruined Puss's old life, and Puss only abandoned him once he realized what Humpty did to him. And he makes it known with several of his actions to manipulate Puss in the movie's present, like getting him unconscious in the desert and drawing the attention of crows to him.

tropes.name: Actionized Sequel
tropes.html: Due to advances in CGI, premiering a year after Shrek Forever After (in a franchise then eleven years in the making), and shifting the focus to the show-stealing swashbuckler, the action sequences are more detailed and frequent than in the mainline Shrek films.

tropes.name: Adam Westing
tropes.html: Antonio Banderas is simply lampooning himself and his past portrayal of Zorro in playing Puss.

tropes.name: Adaptational Villainy
tropes.html: Humpty Dumpty and Jack & Jill are only neutral at best in their origin stories. Here, Humpty starts out as a jerk (both as a child and an adult) who turns out to be masterminding absolutely everything that present day Puss is dealing with and Jack & Jill are an Obviously Evil duo with pretty much no real standards who receive a well-deserved crushing from the Golden Goose's mother.

tropes.name: Addressed by the Baby
tropes.html: Parodied when Jack and Jill are pretending that their pet warthog Hamhock is their baby son, and Jack says, "Did you hear that? I think he just called me 'daddy'!"

tropes.name: Alien Blood
tropes.html: Watch carefully in the flashback when Puss and Humpty become blood brothers. Humpty has yolk instead of blood, naturally.

tropes.name: Amusingly Short List
tropes.html: The secret "bean club" devoted to looking for magic beans has only one rule, not to talk about it, which is stated twice.

tropes.name: Arbitrary Skepticism
tropes.html: Despite the 'verse being a Fantasy Kitchen Sink, Jack and the Beanstalk is considered a myth, but only because Puss has had no way to verify it.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html: "You are better than this."

tropes.name: Arrested for Heroism
tropes.html: Even though Puss did save San Ricardo from the Giant Goose and the people considered him a hero, he's still considered an outlaw and the soldiers still try to arrest him at the end of the movie, forcing Puss to leave town.

tropes.name: Attack of the 50-Foot Whatever
tropes.html: The mother goose.

tropes.name: Badass Adorable
tropes.html: Puss, as usual, and also Kitty Softpaws. Particularly Puss as a kitten, look at his little belly!

tropes.name: Bad Guy Bar
tropes.html: Puss visits one at the beginning of the film.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch Comment
tropes.html: "You are not as good as they say you are, Miss Softpaws — you're better."

tropes.name: Bar Brawl
tropes.html: More like Bar Dance Brawl, and it later plays into a swordfight.

tropes.name: Battle Couple
tropes.html: Puss and Kitty; Jack and Jill.

tropes.name: Berserk Button
tropes.html: Don't even get one drop of milk on Puss' boots. During the dance fight, this is the moment when the dance fight becomes a Sword Fight.

tropes.name: Big Bad Friend
tropes.html: Humpty was the Big Bad the entire time. Although later in the movie, he redeems himself and is on Puss's side again.

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html:
Many, as the movie is set in an alternate-universe Spain.
  • Yet this one takes the prize — literally, "Damned egg". Made even better by the fact that huevo is also used as an euphemism for testicle.
    Puss: [referring to Humpty Dumpty] Maldito huevo...
  • When the tattooed man offers to show Puss his tattoos of "the golden eggs" and goes for his fly, to Puss's horror. As stated above, the Spanish word for "egg" is also slang for "testicle," making this at least an implied bilingual pun.
  • You also get a relatively rare occasion in which the phrase "Holy frijoles!" — often used in a stereotypical fashion in film and TV depictions of Mexicans, or used by non-Mexicans as a generic exclamation in the same context as "Ay Caramba!" —- is actually uttered by a noted Hispanic actor in a non-stereotypical context.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: Kinda. Puss saved San Ricardo and earned his mama's forgiveness, but he's still an outlaw. Though this won't last forever.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html:
• The movie opens and ends with a narration by Puss.
  • Puss and Humpty flee San Ricardo with a horse carriage full of gold in both the flashback and the climax.
  • The movie begins and ends with Puss and Kitty dancing together in almost the same moves.

tropes.name: Carnivore Confusion
tropes.html:
Puss: I should make you into an egg salad sandwich!
Humpty: Yech! That is disgusting!

tropes.name: Cat Ninja
tropes.html: The cats (in particular Kitty Softpaws) are sometimes portrayed in a very ninjaesque way.<!-- This example needs more context. what is "ninjaesque"?-->

tropes.name: Cats Are Mean
tropes.html: Played somewhat unconventionally in that most of the feline characters in the flick are only smarmy or jerks to those that really deserve it.

tropes.name: Cats Are Snarkers
tropes.html: Kitty Softpaws easily qualifies; Puss himself might to a lesser extent.

tropes.name: Cats Hate Water
tropes.html: Zigzagged — Puss is shown taking a leap into a river during the flashback, but a prison guard can keep him in line with just a spray bottle. This is actually similar to the way cats behave in real life — most will enter water without a fuss if they need or want to, but they hate having it thrown on them against their will.

tropes.name: Cephalothorax
tropes.html: Humpty.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html: Both Humpty's original glider (the one built in childhood) and the flying carriage end up being used during the climax.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Skill
tropes.html: Puss and Kitty's dancing pops up on several occasions.

tropes.name: Classy Cat-Burglar
tropes.html: Salma Hayek's character, literally. She's able to steal Puss's hat AND boots without Puss realizing it!

tropes.name: Combat Pragmatist
tropes.html: When Softpaws makes him lose his sword in their fight, Puss has no problem hitting her with a guitar. Softpaws doesn't let him live that one down.

tropes.name: Cool Mask
tropes.html: Kitty has a black luchador-style one.

tropes.name: Cool Sword
tropes.html: Puss has an ornate rapier, but Kitty does one better with a size-retractable dagger.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
tropes.html: The Commandante is voiced by Guillermo del Toro, the film's producer.

tropes.name: Cub Cues Protective Parent
tropes.html: The Goose that lays the Golden Eggs turns out to be the gosling of a gargantuan goose, who is not too keen about having her offspring stolen.

tropes.name: Cute Giant
tropes.html: The Golden Goose's mother.

tropes.name: Cut the Safety Rope
tropes.html: When Puss is holding the two ropes—one holding the Golden Goose and the other holding Humpty—from the edge of the cliff, Humpty spares him having to make the decision of whether he will save his brother, or save the town by saving the Goose, by letting go off the rope.

tropes.name: Dance Battler
tropes.html: Both Puss and Kitty during their first duel.

tropes.name: Dance of Romance
tropes.html: Subverted in Puss and Kitty's first "dance" due to Puss being unaware his opponent is female; played straighter in their dance after retrieving the Golden Goose, which is much more intimate.

tropes.name: Dance Party Ending
tropes.html: It's a Shrek tradition, this time set to Lady Gaga's "Americano".

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: Unlike the series it was spun off from, which was a comedy with a bit of drama mixed in, this movie is more of an action/comedy.

tropes.name: Dashing Hispanic
tropes.html: Both Puss and Kitty are mask-wearing stylish swashbucklers that give a heavy Zorro vibe.

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html:
Kitty Softpaws
Puss: Do not worry. I will protect you.
Kitty: What are you gonna do? Hit it in the head with a guitar?

tropes.name: Defecting for Love
tropes.html: Kitty starts out as Puss's rival and is in on Humpty's plot against him, but ultimately ends up as his Love Interest.

tropes.name: Disney Death
tropes.html: Humpty topples off a bridge and supposedly dies, but the epilogue shows that he recovers.

tropes.name: Dramatic Spotlight
tropes.html: Spotlights follow Puss and Kitty around during their confrontation at the Glitter Box, highlighting the action. It is mostly downplayed, since the area outside the spotlights is just dim, not pitch black, although there are some moments that turn up the contrast, like the spotlight on Kitty when Puss first spots her and as he approaches.

tropes.name: DreamWorks Face
tropes.html: From Humpty rather than the actual lead.

tropes.name: Dung Fu
tropes.html: In a Funny Background Event, Jill mentions a Noodle Incident in which she and Jack adopted a monkey and all it did was throw poo all over the place.

tropes.name: Early Personality Signs
tropes.html: Puss is shown as a kitten fighting off some schoolyard bullies and meowing with a war cry inflection. As a full-grown cat, he's a martial artist.

tropes.name: Emotional Language Shift
tropes.html: Puss and Kitty lapse into Spanish when in an emotional state.

tropes.name: Et Tu, Brute?
tropes.html: "Kitty? Not you too." - A heartbroken Puss realizes that she was in on the whole thing herself.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Loved Ones
tropes.html: Jack and Jill are by all means ruthless bandits, but are Happily Married and treat their hogs like children.

tropes.name: Evil All Along
tropes.html: Kitty, the drinkers at the bar and the white cat from the start were secretly part of the Big Bad's scheme. Also, the Big Bad was Humpty Dumpty, which gets revealed in a Wham Shot.

tropes.name: Face–Heel Turn
tropes.html: Humpty gets a bit too into his dream of finding the golden eggs, and what once began as an innocent dream turns into an unhealthy obsession when he grows older. Enough for the Reveal in the movie to be that Humpty orchestrated the whole plot, thereby turning Puss into the outlaw once again. However, later in the movie after Puss is angry at him for betraying him, he becomes Puss' friend again and even tries to help him out at the end.

tropes.name: Femme Fatale
tropes.html: Kitty. Also, the white cat Puss is implied to have slept with at the very beginning, who turns out to have been on Humpty's payroll.

tropes.name: Flashback
tropes.html: A lengthy one is given by Puss to explain to Kitty (and the audience) the extent of his relationship with Humpty Dumpty.

tropes.name: Forced Dance Partner
tropes.html: At one point, Humpty and the Golden Goose are dancing, while Puss and Kitty are also dancing. Humpty at one point makes them swap partners against their will.

tropes.name: Foregone Conclusion
tropes.html:
• Anybody who has been on the Shrek 4D ride at Universal Studios would have seen Humpty Dumpty's apparent death coming, as Donkey accidentally knocks over his grave marker in the cemetery scene.
  • Kitty Softpaws is nowhere to be seen or even mentioned in the main ''Shrek'' series.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
• Humpty Dumpty, upon finding the Golden Goose's "nest", remarks that he feels like he belongs there, and later remarks that he didn't feel like he belonged in San Ricardo much less anywhere. He turns out to be a golden egg given life.
  • Also, when Jack says that’s "their cue" after finding Humpty's telescope and seeing the beanstalk chopped down, things feel like Humpty was the one responsible for the whole thing.
  • Adding on to that, Humpty gets very cross with Kitty every time she becomes closer to Puss and separates them; at one point, he warns her not to get too close to Puss and “stick to the plan”. This is because Humpty turned out to be Evil All Along and was planning on double-crossing Puss from the start.

tropes.name: Freeze-Frame Bonus
tropes.html: One of the orphans at the San Ricardo Orphanage is Mary and her little lamb.

tropes.name: Friend-or-Idol Decision
tropes.html: An unusual case, in which the friend sacrifices themselves so the hero can get the idol.

tropes.name: Full Moon Silhouette
tropes.html: While being chased by Puss, Kitty Softpaws leaps off a roof, passing in front of the moon.

tropes.name: Furry Reminder
tropes.html: Similar to the previous movies, while Puss is more or less a swashbuckling hero, he can't overcome his feline instincts.

tropes.name: Gambit Roulette
tropes.html: EVERY event up to the climax at San Ricardo was Humpty's gambit for revenge.

tropes.name: Genre Shift
tropes.html: The regular Shrek series was an Affectionate Parody of fairy tales, a trait that's prevalent even through its most serious moments. Puss's story in the 'verse keeps the irreverent sense of fairy tale humor (in a lesser amount) but has a much more action-orientated tone similar to Pirates of the Caribbean.

tropes.name: Gigantic Adults, Tiny Babies
tropes.html: The Golden Goose is around the same height as Puss, whereas the Great Terror (the goose's mother) towers over all the buildings of San Ricardo.

tropes.name: Gory Discretion Shot
tropes.html: Subverted. Jack and Jill slam Humpty against a wooden cart by their shadows on a wall, then a crack sound is heard and liquid starts spraying out of Humpty. Turns out it's just a champagne bottle.

tropes.name: Hairball Humor
tropes.html: When Kitty feels bad because Humpty excludes her from their celebration (saying, "Humpty and Puss! We did it!"), she goes to bed early, saying she has a hairball as an excuse.

tropes.name: Half-Dressed Cartoon Animal
tropes.html: Puss and Kitty.

tropes.name: Hand Cannon
tropes.html: Jack and Jill have a literal one — the gun they use is a miniaturized, handheld cannon, complete with a fuse.

tropes.name: Happily Adopted
tropes.html:
• Puss by Imelda. It takes a long time for them to reconcile after Puss becomes an outlaw.
  • If the end credits are to be believed, Mother Goose adopts Humpty.

tropes.name: Heel–Face Revolving Door
tropes.html: Humpty goes through it twice.

tropes.name: Heel–Face Turn
tropes.html: Both Kitty and Humpty go back on their plan to abandon Puss and San Ricardo.

tropes.name: Heist Clash
tropes.html: While trying to steal the magic beans from the outlaws Jack and Jill, Puss is tripped up by another cat (dressed in a black mask and cape) who is also trying to steal the beans. Their scuffle over who has the "right" to steal the beans leads to them being noticed by Jack and Jill and escaping narrowly without the beans. The stranger later reveals herself as attractive cat burglar Kitty Softpaws, leading Puss to revise his negative opinion.

tropes.name: Held Gaze
tropes.html: A very short one, as part of the Mating Dance scene between Puss and Kitty (see example below).

tropes.name: Helium Speech
tropes.html: Puss, Kitty and Humpty speak like this while atop the clouds due to the thin air.

tropes.name: Heroic Sacrifice
tropes.html:
Humpty sacrifices himself so Puss can save the Golden Goose, and thus San Ricardo from her mother's wrath.
Puss: I will not let you go, Humpty.
Humpty: [smiling] I know you won't. So I won't make you choose.

tropes.name: Heterosexual Life-Partners
tropes.html: Puss and Humpty, though it gets muddied for... complicated reasons.

tropes.name: High-Dive Escape
tropes.html: During Puss's flashback to how he and Humpty fell out, Puss abandons Humpty to the guard and leaps of the bridge into the river after the wagon crashes.

tropes.name: High on Catnip
tropes.html: Puss claims his bag of catnip is for his glaucoma.

tropes.name: Hollywood Density
tropes.html: Averted; the golden eggs turn out to be so heavy even taking one would have been difficult. That said, the characters do occasionally handle them as if they were far lighter, but this is more artistic than plot-relevant.

tropes.name: Hypocritical Humor
tropes.html: Puss takes offense at Kitty doing the "litterbox" (a kicking-sand motion with her hind legs) at him, only to turn around and drag his butt on the floor as an equally offensive comeback.

tropes.name: Impact Silhouette
tropes.html: Puss leaves a hole with a perfect outline of himself, feather in his hat included, in a box after trying to swing down on a rope.

tropes.name: Impossible Thief
tropes.html: Kitty. A Running Gag has her steal Puss's hat and boots without him noticing until she points it out. Puss later gets to do this to some guards by making their pants fall down without apparently moving a muscle.

tropes.name: Improvised Parachute
tropes.html: Puss and Kitty use leaves from the giant beanstalk as parachutes to save Humpty and the Golden Goose when they fall from the giant's castle.

tropes.name: Improvised Weapon
tropes.html: Puss uses a guitar to knock Kitty out in their first duel, revealing her identity.<!--* InLoveWithTheMark-->

tropes.name: In Name Only
tropes.html: Has nothing to do with the fairy tale Puss in Boots aside from featuring a clever cat who wears boots.

tropes.name: Inspector Javert
tropes.html: The Comandante of San Ricardo.

tropes.name: It's All About Me
tropes.html: Humpty's main character flaw, and ultimately the cause of Puss becoming an outlaw.

tropes.name: Journey to the Sky
tropes.html: The plot spoofs that of the fairy tale Jack and the Beanstalk. Puss, with the help of old friend Humpty Dumpty, steals the magic beans from Jack (who's an outlaw here) so they can plant them and climb to a castle in the sky where a goose laying golden eggs is said to live.

tropes.name: Jump Scare
tropes.html: A minor one when Humpty says, "Hi, plant" to the little sprout in the desert.

tropes.name: Kirk's Rock
tropes.html: The trio pass in front of a creditable rendered version at one point.

tropes.name: Kissing Discretion Shot
tropes.html: Finally, after all the UST between the two, Kitty and Puss finally kiss. Which is hidden behind Puss's hat which Kitty lifts off his head and holds over their faces. Likely done just the give the two some privacy, though they hadn't really been discreet about their attraction before. Could also count as a (covered up) The Big Damn Kiss, because of the dramatic lighting behind them.

tropes.name: Lactose over Liquor
tropes.html: In the beginning of the movie, Puss enters a bar and orders a shot of leche (Spanish for milk), much to the amusement of the other patrons.

tropes.name: Language Fluency Denial
tropes.html:
When he's caught by Jack while trying to rob him, Puss tries to pretend he doesn't speak English.
Jack: You lookin' for something?
Puss: Uh... no. [chuckles nervously] No hablo ingles?

tropes.name: Latin Lover
tropes.html: Puss prides himself as quite The Casanova.

tropes.name: Logo Joke
tropes.html: The familiar Dreamworks opening animation is accompanied by lively Spanish music, including the sound of a whip-crack which coincides with the boy casting out his fishing line.

tropes.name: Making the Choice for You
tropes.html: When Puss has to choose between saving Humpty and the golden goose from falling, Humpty lets go and falls to his death.

tropes.name: Masked Luchador
tropes.html: Kitty wears a mask like this.

tropes.name: Mating Dance
tropes.html: There is a quite passionate and fast paced one between Kitty and Puss after they retrieve the golden chick from the castle, they literally can barely keep their hands(/paws) off each other! Complete with with a Almost Kiss and even a Held Gaze moment. The "Dance Battle" can be interpreted as this, if one-sided.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: Kitty Softpaws can rob you blind and literally has no claws.

tropes.name: Meet Cute
tropes.html: Despite the fact they were (so it seemed) preparing to fight to the death (and the fact guitar clubbing was included), the first real time Kitty and Puss meet, they seem to have easily over looked that fact, and Puss later expresses his regret over the guitar.

tropes.name: Memento MacGuffin
tropes.html: As it turns out, Puss's hat and boots.

tropes.name: Momma's Boy
tropes.html: Puss has a deep love for his adopted mother Imelda, and outright says that the disappointment in her eyes is what haunts him the most about his Tragic Backstory. His arc in the film concludes with him knowing that he's returned her pride in him.

tropes.name: Monster Is a Mommy
tropes.html: The guardian of the golden goose is actually her gigantic mother. Humpty knew this and stole the goose to bring her mother's wrath down upon San Ricardo.

tropes.name: More Dakka
tropes.html: Hand Cannons? A carriage with broadside cannons? Jack and Jill came down that hill packin'.

tropes.name: My Biological Clock Is Ticking
tropes.html: Hilariously gender-reversed with Jack and Jill, as Jack is the one who wants to have kids. He even uses this line at one point.

tropes.name: Mythology Gag
tropes.html:
A couple to Shrek 2:
  • After Puss is arrested and searched, the guard finds catnip among Puss' possessions. This was part of the COPS parody in Shrek 2.
  • The final scene has Puss and Kitty on the run, in what should have been a romantic scene if not for the soldiers attacking them, mirroring a scene in Shrek and Fiona's "honeymoon".
  • Puss again puts on his Puppy-Dog Eyes, this time for a prison guard so he may escape. The score during this part is the same melody played during the first time Puss does it in Shrek 2. It's even on his Wanted poster.

tropes.name: Near-Miss Groin Attack
tropes.html: Puss is running around on rooftops and jumps over a church steeple. He's a bit worried that the steeple will get him in the crotch, but it narrowly misses, and he sighs with relief.

tropes.name: Off Bridge, onto Vehicle
tropes.html: Kitty and Puss leap of the rock formations in the canyon onto Jack and Jill's wagon.

tropes.name: Offscreen Teleportation
tropes.html: Several times. In the bar scene at the beginning, and in a later scene with Jill.

tropes.name: The Old Convict
tropes.html: "Jack" Andy Beanstalk.

tropes.name: Once Done, Never Forgotten
tropes.html: Kitty keeps reminding Puss he hit her in the head with a guitar.

tropes.name: Once More, with Clarity
tropes.html:
Parodied with this scene warning: spoilers ahead.
The Big Bad: You never knew it Puss, but I was always there there there there.

tropes.name: One Last Job
tropes.html:
• Jack wants to retire and start a family after the job is done. Jill however wants to continue the profession.
  • Also Puss. He wants to stop being an outlaw and go back to San Ricardo, but he can't, unless this one last job lets him pay them back.

tropes.name: One-Steve Limit
tropes.html: Averted. The movie boasts both "Jack and Jill" Jack and "Jack and the Beanstalk" Jack. But then subverted when the latter Jack reveals that his real name is Andy Beanstalk, and Jack was a nickname he got saddled with.

tropes.name: Orphanage of Love
tropes.html: Imelda.

tropes.name: Outlaw Couple
tropes.html: Jack and Jill.

tropes.name: Paper-Thin Disguise
tropes.html: Humpty attempts to blend in with the golden eggs in a gold bodysuit. Unfortunately the actual eggs are barely a foot wide. The goose buys into it at least once, though. Ironically enough, he turns out to be a golden egg himself underneath his normal eggshell.

tropes.name: Partially Civilized Animal
tropes.html: The normal cats in the Glitter Box have their own bar and musicians, but different from Puss in Boots and Kitty Softpaws, they walk on fours, do not talk, and are more animalistic.

tropes.name: Pop-Star Composer
tropes.html: Rodrigo y Gabriela did additional music for the film, teaming up with Hans Zimmer protege Henry Jackman.

tropes.name: Prequel
tropes.html: To Shrek 2, the first appearance of the title character.

tropes.name: Prison Rape
tropes.html: Very heavily implied to have happened to Humpty when he was in prison. "It ain't over easy" indeed.

tropes.name: Pungeon Master
tropes.html:
Humpty Dumpty is usually surrounded by egg puns.
Humpty: Do you know what they do to eggs in prison? I'll tell you this much... it ain't over easy.

tropes.name: Red Eyes, Take Warning
tropes.html: Jack and Jill's boars have glowing red eyes, as does the mother goose in a brief shot.

tropes.name: Redemption Equals Death
tropes.html: Puss manages to appeal to the good still in Humpty, who ends up performing a Heroic Sacrifice to save the golden goose (and by extension, San Ricardo).

tropes.name: Revenge
tropes.html: Humpty's entire plan was to lead Puss back to San Ricardo so he could be locked up (as revenge for "betraying" him), and to also lead the Golden Goose's mother there to destroy the whole town (as revenge for locking him up).

tropes.name: Revenge Myopia
tropes.html: Humpty's big grievance against Puss is the fact that Puss abandoned him to the authorities after the failed robbery of the bank. Humpty seems unwilling to recognize that he is just as guilty by tricking Puss into aiding him against his explicit wishes, and ruined his hard-earned reputation as the town hero in the process. He doesn't even view what he did as a betrayal, thinking that Puss was just supposed to go along with it because they're blood-brothers.

tropes.name: Ridiculously Cute Critter
tropes.html: The Golden Goose. Kitty Softpaws and Puss also qualify.

tropes.name: Roof Hopping
tropes.html: Quite a bit, mostly from Puss and Kitty.

tropes.name: Running Gag
tropes.html:
• Kitty stealing Puss's things without him noticing.
  • Jack pestering Jill about having kids.
  • Pointing out that Puss In Boots turned a guitar into an improvised weapon.
  • The cat that keeps covering its mouth whenever someone says a pun (or does something naughty) and goes "ooooooo...".

tropes.name: Running on All Fours
tropes.html: Kitty, especially when jumping.

tropes.name: Samus Is a Girl
tropes.html: Kitty, who for the first few minutes of her appearance wears a heavy black mask to hide her face. Given the generally realistic cat proportions the only real thing marking her as a different gender anyway is her voice (at least to the audience. Puss has no problem telling by her face, even though he seems incapable of identifying a female cat otherwise, apparently).

tropes.name: Senior Sleep-Cycle
tropes.html: Jack and the Beanstalk's Jack.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: Shares a page with the rest of the Shrek franchise.

tropes.name: Sigh of Love
tropes.html: At the beginning, Puss is strongly implied to have slept with a Persian molly named Rosa, who he swears he will never forget (a moment he ruins via his Accidental Misnaming of her). When he rides off into the sunset, she sighs wistfully.

tropes.name: Signature Headgear
tropes.html: Puss has a Musketeer-esque hat, complete with feather.

tropes.name: Signature Style
tropes.html: Despite Guillermo del Toro merely producing, a couple of his trademarks like Steampunk (Jack and Jill's cannon carriage, Humpty's transforming carriage) and fantastically improbable creatures (the mother goose) appear in this movie. Not to mention that it's the first work since Pan's Labyrinth that's set in a remotely Hispanic setting.

tropes.name: Signs of Disrepair
tropes.html: There's a bar called the Glitter Box, only the G in the neon sign isn't working.

tropes.name: So Proud of You
tropes.html: Imelda says this to Puss after he saves San Ricardo from the golden goose's mother.

tropes.name: Spaghetti Western
tropes.html: The script, the visual style and even the music all owe a debt to the work of Sergio Leone and his imitators.

tropes.name: Speed, Smarts and Strength
tropes.html:
Humpty Dumpty's Dream Team for the Cloud Castle heist consists of himself (brains), Puss (brawn), and Kitty (speed). Technically, both Kitty and Puss are great fighters but Kitty is consistently shown to be a tick faster.
Humpty: Look, with Kitty's skill, your sword and my brain, we've got a fighting chance here.

tropes.name: Stalker Shot
tropes.html: Shows up in the flashback scenes as Humpty Dumpty reveals he's been setting up Puss-In-Boots and has actually been present at several important points in story, often in some ludicrous disguise.

tropes.name: The Starscream
tropes.html: Jack and Jill turn on Humpty at the end. Of course, Humpty had pulled a Heel–Face Turn by then, so it may be a subversion.

tropes.name: Steampunk
tropes.html: Jack and Jill's wagon-cannons, Humpty's glider-wagon.

tropes.name: Stealth Pun
tropes.html:
• Lil Boy Blue is literally a Blue Meanie.
  • Let's see, Humpty is smart, inventive, and was incredibly imaginative as a child. He's literally an Egg Head.
  • Also, his flashback where he is "everywhere" Puss was in the movie makes him an Easter Egg.

tropes.name: Stopped Dead in Their Tracks
tropes.html: After Puss in Boots confronts Humpty Dumpty over their history, he starts to leave in anger. Just then, Humpty mentions how bad prison life was for him. This stops Puss in his tracks for a bit, but eventually he continues walking away.

tropes.name: Swallow the Key
tropes.html: Jack swallows the key that locks the box where the magic beans are kept.

tropes.name: Taken for Granite
tropes.html: According to Humpty, anyone who looks at the monster in the castle will turn to stone. This is a lie and is only meant to keep Puss and Kitty from finding out that the monster is the Goose's mother.

tropes.name: Talking Animal
tropes.html: Puss and Kitty.<!--* ThatPoorCat-->

tropes.name: This Cannot Be!
tropes.html:
[the Cat in Black dances towards Puss, makes a defiant growl, and ducks below camera]
Puss: [aghast] How dare you do the Litter Box on me!

tropes.name: Toothy Bird
tropes.html: The mother goose. Actually reminiscent of real-life geese, which have serrated beaks.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Lie
tropes.html:
• A scene from the commercials where Puss uses his Puppy-Dog Eyes to repel a thrown dagger is nowhere to be found in the film proper.
  • Puss's Overly Long Gag with sipping the leche... he still does it in the actual movie, but it's no longer a long gag, and he doesn't say, "I'm still thirsty" after finishing.
  • The running gag with the cat that goes "Ooh...!" has him taking his hand out of his mouth after Puss scolds him, which doesn't happen in the actual movie.

tropes.name: Triggered by the Name
tropes.html: When Puss is in jail with Andy "Jack" Beanstalk, Jack tells him not to mention Humpty Dumpty's name, since Jack and Humpty used to be cellmates and Jack hates Humpty.

tropes.name: True Companions
tropes.html: Puss and Humpty, when they were kids, and considered each other "brothers". Not so much in the present, though Humpty tries to get it back or at least pretends to, in order to take revenge. However, Puss manages to appeal to the good still in him, and they seem to be friends again right before Humpty's death.

tropes.name: Two Guys and a Girl
tropes.html: Puss, Humpty, and Kitty form this dynamic.

tropes.name: Used to Be a Sweet Kid
tropes.html: Humpty Dumpty.

tropes.name: Unresolved Sexual Tension
tropes.html: Very much so between Puss and Kitty through most of the movie.

tropes.name: Visual Pun
tropes.html:
• First off, Humpty admitting that he's been a "rotten egg". Then after his Heroic Sacrifice, his exterior is obliterated to reveal a golden egg, making him a literal Jerk with a Heart of Gold.
  • Let's not forget the tip of the hat to the best known fairy tale mascot of all time — a literal Mother Goose.
  • Puss literally takes the bull by the horn when he takes the initiative towards being a hero.
  • In the Once More, with Clarity sequence, Humpty appears disguised as a cat — a literal cat suit.

tropes.name: Vocal Dissonance
tropes.html: In the flashback, Puss is revealed to have had the same voice he had as an adult... as a kitten. As did Humpty.

tropes.name: The Voiceless
tropes.html: Subverted in the flashback, where a young Puss almost never speaks until near the end of the flashback.

tropes.name: Walk Into Camera Obstruction
tropes.html: With Humpty, when he Puss and Kitty first get into the giant's castle. Humpty, being rolled inside, with his gold disguise fills the screen.

tropes.name: Wardrobe Wound
tropes.html: Puss is fairly restrained during the dance battle against Kitty, until she splashes a single drop of milk on his boot, at which point he draws his rapier and tries to kill her.

tropes.name: We Used to Be Friends
tropes.html: Puss and Humpty.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html: Little Boy Blue is never heard from again. In a Deleted Scene, he appears briefly as an adult.

tropes.name: What Measure Is a Non-Cute?
tropes.html: The adorable Puss is praised as a hero and loved like a son by the orphanage matron while his childhood friend Humpty, who is pretty much just a big face, is regularly mocked, gets into much trouble, and is the true antagonist of the film.

tropes.name: What the Hell, Hero?
tropes.html:
A comical example with Puss during the dance fight. After Puss hits Kitty (not knowing she is a woman at first) with a guitar, she unmasks herself and yells at him for it.
Kitty: You hit me in the head with a GUITAR?!

tropes.name: Where It All Began
tropes.html: The story eventually leads back to Puss' hometown of San Ricardo. Of course, this turns out to be intentional, as part of Humpty's revenge plot.

tropes.name: Wistful Smile
tropes.html:
Puss smiles sadly after Humpty sacrifices himself to save the Golden Goose, revealing himself to be a golden egg on the inside.
Puss: I always knew you were good inside.

tropes.name: Who's Laughing Now?
tropes.html: Invoked word for word (barring the accent) when the castle in the clouds is proven to be real.

tropes.name: Your Approval Fills Me with Shame
tropes.html: Kitty has this moment when Humpty gives her a golden egg. She felt nothing but guilt and shame for betraying Puss and realize that the gold doesn't matter anymore because she loved Puss more.

tropes.name: You Are Better Than You Think You Are
tropes.html: The Arc Words for this movie. Puss uses this to set Humpty right.

tropes.name: Animal Gender-Bender
tropes.html: Gonzalo is a male tortoiseshell cat. While it's possible with X-chromosome duplication, having three sex chromosomes comes with a host of other symptoms.

tropes.name: Arson, Murder, and Jaywalking
tropes.html: "Fooood..." "Waterrrr...." "Toiler paper..." Puss then gives himself a hasty wash across the touch zone.

tropes.name: Big "NO!"
tropes.html: Puss gives one when The Whisperer tries to kill the Three Diablos, who saved his life after their Heel–Face Turn.

tropes.name: Cats Are Mean
tropes.html: Initially played with, then subverted.

tropes.name: Cat Stereotype
tropes.html: Gonzalo is a tortoiseshell cat whom Puss named for his scrappy temper.

tropes.name: Cute Kitten
tropes.html: The titular kittens.

tropes.name: Disney Villain Death
tropes.html: The Whisperer falls into a ravine during the fight with Puss and the Diablos.

tropes.name: The Ditz
tropes.html: Sir Timoteo Montenegro III (a.k.a. Timmy).

tropes.name: Epic Flail
tropes.html: The Whisperer's weapon.

tropes.name: Face of an Angel, Mind of a Demon
tropes.html: Initially played straight for the kittens, then subverted. See Heel–Face Turn.

tropes.name: Flat "What"
tropes.html: Puss has this reaction when he makes his signature face and the kittens respond by doing the same.<!--* FurryReminder: The kittens.-->

tropes.name: Gender Equals Breed
tropes.html: Subverted. Although the title character is a male orange tabby, Gonzalo is a male calico. He even has a sister, Perla, who has a cream tabby pattern as orange, cream, and (the rare anyway) apricot colors are, although neither rare, let alone improbable on female cats, more common on male cats.

tropes.name: Heel–Face Turn
tropes.html: Puss helps the kittens away from being the Whisperer's minions, having learned from his experiences in his movie.<!--* KillerRabbit: Still the kittens.--><!--* TheSpeechless: The titular kittens again.-->

tropes.name: Skyward Scream
tropes.html:
After Puss is buried alive from the Diablos and manages to get free.
Puss: [furious] Pray for mercy... DIABLOOOOOOOOOOS!!!!!!

tropes.name: Tasty Gold
tropes.html: On giving the kittens each a gold coin, Gonzalo and Perla bite theirs to check its authenticity. Timoteo sees what they're doing and, misinterpreting the situation, eats his own.

tropes.name: Two Guys and a Girl
tropes.html: Gonzalo (male), Timoteo (male), and Perla (female).

title: The Evil Dead

accept.reason: Released October 15, 1981 (IMDb tt0083907, 1981); TMDB dates movie 764 by its 1983 release, so the year rule rejects it

intro: The Evil Dead is a horror film that marks the first chapter of the Evil Dead franchise. It was written and directed by Sam Raimi, and released on October 15, 1981. The first film's story follows five Michigan State University students (Bruce Campbell, Ellen Sandweiss, Rich De Manincor, Betsy Baker, and Theresa Tilly) who decide to spend a weekend at a very dilapidated cabin in rural Tennessee. Whi

tropes.name: Action Survivor
tropes.html: In contrast to the sequels establishing him as a manly badass, Ash here is a normal young man who is not Made of Iron, a One-Man Army or Gadgeteer Genius and has to suddenly fight off his friends being demonically possessed.

tropes.name: All Just a Dream
tropes.html: The Comic-Book Adaptation ends with Ash waking up in the car pulling up to the cabin with only Linda to explain the discrepancies between the first two movies. Ash vs. Evil Dead renders this non-canon, though, as it firmly establishes that everyone in the first movie was present at the cabin in the official continuity.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html: Join... Us!

tropes.name: Attack! Attack! Attack!
tropes.html: Part of what makes the film so frightening is that the Deadites do not let up- once the characters unleash the evil into the woods, the Deadites continue to assault them until morning. They even continue the assault in broad daylight, which catches Ash unaware and leads to a Bolivian Army Ending.

tropes.name: B-Movie
tropes.html: Definitely among the most famous B Movies ever.

tropes.name: Bigger on the Inside
tropes.html: The cabin might as well be a TARDIS.

tropes.name: Blonde, Brunette, Redhead
tropes.html: Cheryl (blonde), Shelly (brunette) and Linda (redhead).

tropes.name: Bloody Horror
tropes.html:
• Once Ash goes into the basement, the house starts to bleed. It pours from the plumbing, the electrical sockets, into a lightbulb, and drips onto a projector that paints a striking red image on the wall as Ash walks by.
  • The shot of blood dripping down over the camera as Scotty dismembers Shelly was added specifically as a Literal Metaphor in response to producer Irvin Shapiro's advice to Raimi before filming that he "Keep the blood runnin' down the screen!"

tropes.name: Bolivian Army Ending
tropes.html: After everything he goes through, and having seemingly defeated the evil, the last shot of the movie sees Ash aggressively ambushed by the same Evil Force that possessed all of the other characters. Thankfully, we know from the sequels that he lives to kick all kinds of ass, but you'd have no reason to guess that from here.

tropes.name: Bowdlerize
tropes.html: The British Board of Film Classification would not approve the release of the film without some of the goriest moments being edited out, and after it became Public Enemy #1 of the Video Nasties controversy anyway, they demanded further cuts in order to allow it to return. While the censored version was still incredibly gory (there wasn't really any way around that), the impact of the violence was lessened somewhat by removing all moments where one character stabs or strikes another repeatedly, and all shots of blood gushing from wounds were edited out.

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html: When Ash presents his gift to Linda, he pretends to sleep and only opens his eyes when Linda isn't looking at him. Later, when Ash digs a grave for Linda's Deadite, she is actually Playing Possum and only opens its eyes when Ash isn't paying attention.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• The rickety bridge the group drives over to get to the cabin. A couple of planks fall off it as they drive - and sure enough it's either collapsed by itself or (more likely) has been torn apart by the Evil by the time Cheryl wants to leave.
  • That cheap magnifying glass pendant Ash gifts to Linda? Ash uses it to get ahold of the Necronomicon.

tropes.name: Comic-Book Adaptation
tropes.html: Dark Horse Comics published a four-issue adaptation in 2008

tropes.name: Covers Always Lie
tropes.html: Much of the promotional material for the film originates from a photoshoot (see images 326-341 here) from early 1982 - several years after actual shooting wrapped - in which Bruce Campbell participated but none of the other actors did, resulting in an Ash who is visibly older with different haircut, a female lead (actress Bridget Hoffman) who is clearly not in the movie, and situations which never occur- such as Ash fending off a Deadite with a chainsaw while his co-star cowers behind him, or most famously, the woman being dragged underground by a demonic hand.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
tropes.html: Hinted at by the tape: "Saman sa'rob dar ees haikar dande roza", this being derived from "Sam [Raimi] and Rob [Tapert] are hitchhikers on the road." Sure enough, if you paid attention five minutes into the film, Scott drove the Olds past a pair of idiotic-looking hitchhikers in fishing gear, both of whom turn to wave as the car speeds by.

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html: While nowhere near the jokester he'd be in future installments, Ash still has his moments — such as dryly remarking "Truly amazing" after Linda "guesses" a card in the psychic game she and Shelly play.

tropes.name: Decoy Protagonist
tropes.html: Early on, Scott is the most heroic and proactive of the characters, and Cheryl is the one who most clearly fits the Final Girl archetype. Ash, meanwhile, is a next to useless Distressed Dude who gets trapped under falling bookshelves and overall looks like prime Red Shirt material. This quickly changes.

tropes.name: Developing Doomed Characters
tropes.html: Often credited as being the Trope Maker in the horror genre, as the first 20-30 minutes of the film are dedicated to focusing on the cast before the demons start attacking. Unlike most examples, however, the characters here are likeable (if a bit flat) and there's tremendous use of tension building right from the start.

tropes.name: Disproportionate Retribution
tropes.html: All Ash and Scott did was find the book and a tape deck and played it. Because of that, they summoned demons from Hell to possess everyone and almost everyone dies.

tropes.name: Dramatic Curtain Toss
tropes.html:
• Scottie slowly lifts every curtain in his girlfriend's room after she goes he missing. Each time, he anticipates her being there, only to find nothing.
  • In the finale, Ash starts to catch wise and aim his rifle at the curtain in the same room when he thinks one of his demon-possessed friends is hiding there. They're actually hiding right outside the window near the curtain.

tropes.name: Early-Installment Weirdness
tropes.html:
• The professor refers to the book of the dead as "Naturom Demonto" rather than "Necronomicon". The 2013 remake thus called it by its original name. Evil Dead Rise explains that there are three different copies of the Book of the Dead: the Necronomicon (which Ash's adventures officially dealt with), Natorum Demonto (retconned into being the book Mia and her friends dealt with), and the unnamed third copy that causes the plot of Rise.
  • The "Naturom Demonto" is smaller than all other representations of the evil books in future installments. It is an octavo, about the size of a modern trade paperback, while all other representations are quartos, about the size of a modern coffee table book.
  • This is the most straight-laced horror film of the series aside from the remake with very little comedy to be found, if any at all. Ash's further adventures in Evil Dead 2, Army of Darkness, and Ash vs. Evil Dead get increasingly wacky with Three Stooges-esque comedy.
  • Ash is much more humble and down to earth in this movie, a contrast to the cocky, one-liner spewing Genius Ditz in the sequels, though he does get in a touch of his familiar sarcasm. His iconic "Groovy" Catchphrase is likewise absent. Furthermore, he doesn't utilize his iconic weapons in this film: while Ash does rev up the chainsaw, he never properly uses it as a weapon until the later films. He does use a shotgun in this film, but it's is an unmodified single-barrel shotgun unlike his signature double-barreled shotgun that he saws off in Evil Dead 2.
  • Deadite possession is implied to be fatal to its victims, with the Deadite versions of Cheryl and Scotty disintegrating into goo when they're freed from the demonic influence. In most future Evil Dead entries it's possible (albeit very rare) for people to be freed from possession, though Evil Dead Rise would later depict Deadite possession in a manner more akin to this film.

tropes.name: Endearingly Dorky
tropes.html: In this movie, Ash is nerdy and constantly trips over his words, puts his foot in his mouth, and isn't much of an action hero, but Linda seems to like him for all these reasons.

tropes.name: Ending Fatigue
